To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the selectivity of a monoclonal dimer for a macroporous strong cation exchange resin increases with salt concentration and that this behavior can be predicted by a shrinking core model.

(1) the selectivity of a dimer over its monomeric species on a cation exchanger is a strong function of the salt concentration in the mobile phase and the protein load on the stationary phase, (2) the adsorption kinetics of the two species are similar and controlled by pore diffusion at high protein load and strong binding conditions, and (3) the adsorption equilibrium of the dimer is more sensitive to changes in salt concentration than that of the monomer.
the adsorption equilibrium of mAb monomer and dimes on cation exchange resin depends on salt concentration and that adsorption kinetics can be predicted by a dual shrinking-core model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a model that predicts the equilibrium and kinetics of the adsorption of protein mixtures on a chromatography resin.

the adsorption equilibrium and kinetics for a monoclonally derived immunoglobulin (mAb) and its dimeric form on a macropore cation exchange resin in the dilute limit under salt gradient elution conditions and at high protein loadings.
the development of a new chromatography method for the separation of protein aggregates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the dimer/ monomer selectivity in salt gradient elution is determined by the relative binding strengths and the binding strength is determined by the local concentration of the salt ions in the pores.
the dimer/ monomer selectivity is strongly dependent on the protein load and salt concentration.
the selectivity between dimer and monomer mAbs is strongly influenced by the protein load and the salt concentration in the buffer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

at low salt concentrations and weak binding conditions (dilute limit), dimer/monomeric selectivity is high and the kinetics is controlled by mass transfer, whereas at high salt concentrations and strong binding conditions, the selectivity is low and the kinetics is still controlled by mass transfer.
the dimer/ monomer selectivity is controlled primarily by the salt concentration, and that the dimer is the dominant species in the high salt region.

dimer/monomeric mAb adsorption selectivity in salt gradient elution can be tuned over a wide range by varying protein loading and salt concentration, that the selectivity in dilute limit conditions is controlled by electrostatic interactions between the protein molecules and the cation exchange resin, and that the selectivity at high protein loads is controlled by the protein-protein interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the dimer/ monomer selectivity can be controlled in a wide range by the salt concentration and the binding strength, and the kinetics of the adsorption of the mixtures is controlled by pore-diffusion and can be predicted by a shrinking core model.
the dimer/mono selectivity in the dilute limit is much lower than at high protein loads, and this can be used to separate the dimer and monomer species in the dilute and concentrated limit.

the dimer/ monomer selectivity can be manipulated by changing the salt concentration and that the dimeric species can be separated from the monomer species at high protein loads under strong binding conditions.
